en: Commentary on the Separate Biography of the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai, Volume One.
Annotated by the Śramaṇa Tanzhao of Siming.
The *Biographical Record of the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai*:

"Tiantai" is the name of the mountain; the posthumous title of the Patriarch will be explained in detail below. As for the term "separate" (*bie*), it is so named in contrast to the "comprehensive" (*zong*).
The comprehensive version consists of the thirty-fascicle *Continued Biographies* by Nanshan, arranged into ten sections; this present work is extracted from that comprehensive record.
There are four different versions. First, the record by Zhāng'ān; second, the record by Fǎlùn of Yùquán; third, the record by Zhìguǒ of Huìkē;
and fourth, the record by Fǎlín of Lóngtián Monastery on Mount Zhōngnán. All four of these individuals were disciples of the Great Master;
however, only that which was recorded by Zhāng'ān has circulated in the world, while the other three have long been unheard of. What a pity!
Alas, it is lost! As for what is called "transmission" (chuán, *qùshēng*): it is transmitted through one's deeds and conduct so that it does not perish for ten thousand generations.
According to Cui Bao’s *Gǔjīn Zhù*, Cheng Jia asked: "What is this 'transmission'? He replied:
"All transmissions are made of wood, one foot five inches in length. One writes the talismanic seal (*fúxìn*) upon it and seals it with another board; all are [reserved] for the Emperor."
It means "transmitting the truth. Now, the two teachings of Confucianism and Buddhism record good and evil deeds in written compilations, which serve eternally as a mirror for guidance.

The fact that they do not use wooden printing blocks is likewise the meaning of "transmission and communication. Question: The Great Master [Zhiyi] appeared during the Chen and Sui dynasties, while Nanshan [Daoxuan] was born in the Tang dynasty.
Why can it be said that "the general gives rise to the particular"? Answer: Although the *Continued Biographies* (Xu chuan) produced by Nanshan appeared later, [it follows the same principle].
He then searched for the superior streams [of various traditions] and compiled them into a single collection;

the Master’s own deeds were also included therein, thereby enabling the work to form a comprehensive whole. Recently, there has been a commentary on this edition by Dharma Master Zhichen of Guangfu Monastery at Hexi in Wuxing.
That which is correct shall be preserved; that which is not shall be discarded.

For this purpose, I have now utilized the *General Biographies of Nanshan*, the *One Hundred Records of Tiantai*, the *History of the Southern Dynasties* by Chen Shiseng, the *Biography and Stele Inscription for the Practice of Yuquan* (along with the *Record of the Guanwang Shrine* by Minister Zhang of the Imperial Court), the *Annals and Biographies* of the *Book of Sui*, and the records inscribed on the walls of the Hall that I once read while residing at Yuquan with the fellow practitioner Xun Yunshui.
I have recorded [these matters], citing and annotating everything that was not included in the *Biézhuan* (Separate Biographies),
so that the deeds and conduct of the Patriarchs may shine brilliantly throughout ten thousand generations— an enduring transmission without end.
Compiled by the Disciple Guanding.
"Disciple" refers to one who has entered the gate and the inner chamber to study under a master. The *Biographies of Monks* states: His name was Guanding; his courtesy name was Fayun.
His secular surname was Wu, and he was a native of Wuxing in Changzhou. His ancestors had fled to Dong’ou to escape turmoil and did not return;
consequently, he became a resident of Zhang’an in Linhai. When he was only three months old, his mother wished to name him.

At night, she invoked the names of the Triple Gem, and the infant’s head would follow her lips in imitation; his pronunciation and phrasing were clear and eloquent. At that time, Dharma Master Huizheng of Shejing Temple heard of this.
He sighed and said, "This child is no ordinary person. He was thus named Fanbian (No Ordinary). At the age of seven, he left the household life as a disciple of Master Zheng.
He subsequently sought the Way at Mount Tiantai, where he inherited and practiced meditative concentration and wisdom.

At the age of seventy-two, on the seventh day of the eighth month in the sixth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away at Guoqing Temple. To this day, [his remains] are located south of the main street in front of the temple.
To the east of this place stands a stupa that still exists today. The commentary to the *Book of the Later Han* states that Chang’an County was originally named Ripu;
Emperor Guangwu changed its name to Chang’an. The foundations of the old city walls are located to the southeast of the county.

It is traditionally said that the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) culminates in the "Consecration" (*abhiṣeka*), and the tenth ground (*bhūmi*) culminates in the "Dharma-Cloud" (*dharmamegha*). Having recognized his great capacity, the ordination master [bestowed it upon him]. This must certainly be so.
The people residing on this earth have thus established his name and his style-name.
The Great Master’s taboo name was Zhìyǐ, and his style-name was Dè'ān.
The taboo name of the Patriarch was established by Fǎxù of Guòyuàn Monastery in Xiāngzhōu; *yǐ* means tranquility (*jìng*). As for that—
The Master was thus named De-li.
His surname was Chen.
A *xing* (surname) is that which binds together a lineage for a hundred generations so that it is not confused; a *shi* (clan name) is that which distinguishes descendants.
As for the origin of the Chen clan: according to the *Xingpu* (Genealogical Records), the Chen clan is a surname from Yingchuan in Xuzhou and is listed at the head of the surnames.
Now, based on the "Biography of Chen Shou" in the *Shiji*, when King Wu of Zhou campaigned against Zhou, he sought out the descendants of Shun;
having found Gui Man, he enfeoffed him in Chen to perform the sacrifices to Shun, and he became known as Lord Hu of Chen. From that generation down through the successive dynasties...
Twenty-five rulers possessed the state, down to Chen Min-gong (陳湣公).

This was during the forty-first year of King Jing of Zhou, when the year-stem was *Renxu* (壬戌), and the state was annexed by the state of Chu under King Huai of Chu. In total, this period lasted five hundred and thirty-eight years;
all these rulers were of the Chen clan. As for those in the world today who bear the surname Chen, they likely descend from those who received the clan name when King Wu enfeoffed Gui-man (媯滿).
The place name is uncertain; it is not recorded in various books. Gong Chen claimed he was a descendant of Chen Shi of the Later Han dynasty, but this too lacks evidence.
He was a native of Yingchuan.
Yingchuan Commandery was established during the Qin dynasty and derived its name from a river; "chuan" refers to a watercourse. The *Hou Han zhi* lists the counties of Linying, Yingyin, and Yingyang.

During the Great Song, it was designated as the Jingxi Beilu (Northwest Route of the Capital). In the third year of the Yuanfeng era, it was renamed Yingchang Fu, which corresponds to Xuchang Commandery.
It is located two hundred and fifty li west of the Eastern Capital. It was here that Emperor Xian of the Han dynasty abdicated the throne to the Wei.
Because he was posthumously titled Wǔ (Martial), it was called Xǔchāng; the intention behind this title was the desire that the Han enterprise might flourish once again.
Gāozōng’s magnificent achievements were widely circulated in the genealogical records and histories.
Emperor Gaozong may have been referring to the descendants of Duke Chenhu.
Within these four dynastic histories—the Former and Later Han, Wei, and Jin—there are thirteen individuals who all possess individual biographies. "Mao" signifies greatness; "ji" signifies merit.
When I examined the various histories of Qi, Liang, Chen, and Sui, none contained the ancestral lineage of Chen. This confirms that what Chang'an previously pointed out was far-reaching.
"Generations" refers to family genealogies; "histories" refers to historical records. From the Han through the Jin dynasties, the various lords all achieved great meritorious deeds.
Upon the relocation of the capital during the Jin era, [the lineages were dispersed].
"Ji" means "to reach" or "to arrive at. The Jin Gaozu (High Ancestor) had the surname Sīmǎ, the given name Zī, and the courtesy name Zhòngdá. He was a native of Xiàojì Lǐ in Wēn County, Hé nèi.

He received the abdication of the Wei dynasty and established his capital in Luòyáng. Upon reaching the sixth sovereign, Emperor Mǐn—whose taboo name was Yè and courtesy name Yànfú—he ascended the throne and changed the era name to Jiànxīng.
In the fourth year of this era, he was [assassinated] by Liu Chōng, the King of Hòuzhào, using his younger brother...
Liu Yao besieged and captured Luoyang. No reinforcements arrived from the rest of the realm, and communications between the interior and exterior were severed.

On the *jǐwèi* day of the eleventh month, the Emperor sent the Palace Attendant Song Chǎng to deliver his submission to Yao. The Emperor, riding in a sheep-drawn carriage and baring his right shoulder, went forth to surrender.
He was transferred to Pingyang, and the state was abolished. This reached the seventh sovereign, Emperor Yuán, whose given name was Ruì and courtesy name Jǐngwén.
The capital was moved to Jiankang, which is the present-day city of Jiangning in Shengzhou; it was formerly called Jianye, but was renamed Jiankang to avoid the taboo name of Emperor Min.
My family followed [the court] southward and took up residence along the Yangtze and Han rivers.
The Chen family originally resided in Luo, which is in the north. Jingzhou is in the south; therefore, it is said they "went south. "Yu" means to lodge as a guest.

Because they were fleeing the chaos caused by Liu Yao, they went to the Jiang and Han rivers—"Jiang and Han" refers to the Yangtze and the Han. "Chengzhan" means clear and still; it refers to the water's edge.

This is as stated in the Preface to the "Han Guang" (Broadness of the Han) ode in the *Shijing*: "The Way of King Wen spread throughout the southern states, and his refined culture was put into practice there."
The region of the Yangtze and Han rivers was consequently settled in Huarong County of Jingzhou.
Jingzhou belonged to the Jinghu North Circuit; it is now known as Jiangling Fu. Furthermore, Huarong was changed to Jingmen Jun.
Xian County. The *Hou Han Zhi* states that it was the ancient state of Huāróng, the site of the capital of the state of Chu during the reign of King Ling.

Today, the foundations of the Zhānghuá Terrace still exist there. The *Jiuyou Zhi* states that in the third year of the Qián Dé era, Jian’ning County was established using the territory of Han’s Huāróng;
today it is Gōng’ān County. The present-day Huāróng County of Yuèzhōu is this very place.

His father, Qizǔ, was proficient in the classics and commentaries; his speech was peerless, yet he excelled particularly in military strategy and tactical planning, possessing great courage and decisiveness.
As for the Master’s grandfather, his official rank is unknown, though there exists an inscription for his meritorious deeds approximately one sheet in length.
It is said that he built a monastery to dedicate the merit to his late father, the Governor of Xiangyang. It is likely that [the author] knew the Governor of Xiangyang personally;
he was well-versed in the Five Classics and various dynastic histories, and in his speech, his words were elegant and refined, transcending ordinary human conduct.
Furthermore, his martial arts were perfected, and he was thoroughly versed in the *Sanlue* and *Liutao*. In the application of maneuvers and stratagems, he was certain to achieve victory.

Regarding the art of deploying strategy, Emperor Gaozu of Han said: "In the deployment of strategy within the command tent, and in securing victory a thousand *li* away, I am not equal to Zhang Liang.
(This praises Zhang Liang. Now, this text employs these words to praise him.
Xiangdong Prince Xiao Yi of the Liang dynasty was stationed in Jingzhou and was listed among the guests.
The Liang dynasty had its capital at Jiankang; its ruling house was surnamed Xiao. Its founding ancestor was Emperor Wu, whose personal name was Yan and courtesy name Shuda.
Xiangdong Commandery was precisely Jingzhou. The Prince was the seventh son of Emperor Wu, named Yi, with the courtesy name Shicheng. At first...

The Emperor dreamed of a blind monk holding an incense burner who declared he was to be reborn in the royal palace. Shortly thereafter, while the Emperor’s mother was among the court ladies in attendance, she began to lift her skirt and curtain;
a breeze then blew back her skirt. The Emperor felt a sense of auspicious fortune. One of the ladies dreamed that the moon fell into her womb, and she subsequently became pregnant.
On the day of Ding-si in the eighth month of the seventh year of the Tianjian era, the blind man was born in the inner chambers.
A rare fragrance emanated from within, and there was the anomaly of a purple caul. Emperor Wu marveled at this. At the age of thirteen, he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xiangdong.
Later, he served as the Governor of Jingzhou. In the first year of the Taqing era, he was successively promoted to General Who Guards the West and became the Regional Inspector of Jingzhou.
Among those listed as his guests, Qizǔ was already extraordinary compared to his peers; thus, [the officials] did not dare to treat him as a mere subject. Therefore...
He was appointed as an official guest. This was an official of the Xiangdong Prefecture.

He entered the court by imperial decree, serving as an envoy with the instructions of Prince Xiang. He either offered greetings regarding the weather and the prince’s daily well-being, or conveyed reports.
He was sent as an envoy to the court of Emperor Wu to inquire after the welfare of his fief.
When General-in-Chief Zhu Yi saw him, he sighed and said, "Were it not for one of talent sufficient to govern the state, who else would be so highly esteemed by the Illustrious King?"

*Nanshi*, Biographies, Volume 52. Zhu Yi, courtesy name Yanhe, was a native of Qiantang in Wu Commandery. He was widely learned and possessed great erudition. At the age of twenty-one, he served as an attendant to Ming Shanbin.

Shanbin submitted a memorial recommending him to Emperor Wu, who appointed him as a *boshi* (Master of Scholarly Arts) at the Imperial Academy and concurrently as a *tongshi sheren* (Attendant Official for Ceremonial Matters).
In the eighth year of the Datong era, he was promoted to *shizhong* (Palace Attendant). In the second year of the Taqing era, he became a [Grand Master of Remonstrance].
He continued to hold the office of *lingjun sharen* (Palace Attendant for the Army Command) as before; thus he acquired the title of "Army Commander.
Today, the positions of Shangshu (Minister) and so forth all entail the duties of the Army Commander. At that time, [Zhou] had already begun his career at court, and thus sighed, saying:

"In talent for both the scriptures and statecraft, he is truly a vessel for the highest ministers. Who is he? Who is this? The "Illustrious King" was none other than Prince Xiang, whom [Zhou] did not dare to treat as a subordinate.
Because he was of low rank, he was listed among the guests; thus it is said that [the Emperor] held him in high esteem.

When Emperor Xiaoyuan ascended the throne, in the eighth month of the second year of the Dading era, Hou Jing rebelled. In the third month of the third year, Hou Jing captured Jianye. [The text] notes this.
The Tai City fell; on the fifteenth day of the third month, he ascended the imperial throne at Jingzhou. He was the sixth of the emperors.
He was appointed as Grand Master with Ceremonial Rank and Attendant of the Household, and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Kai-guo County in Yi-yang, holding the rank of *shiji* and *sanqichangshi*.

Regarding the title "Shichijie" (Commissioner with Seal and Authority): Su Wu served as an envoy to the Xiongnu for nineteen years; he returned holding his Han-era seal, and it was based on this precedent that the title "Holding the Seal" (Chijie) was established.
Regarding the "Sanqichangshi" (Attendant Cavalier of the Inner Court): the *Han Guan Yi* states that during the Qin and Former Han dynasties, one Attendant Cavalier was appointed.
As an Attendant Cavalier, one rode alongside the Emperor’s carriage and provided counsel by proposing what was feasible and substituting what was inappropriate.
Wearing the *diao-chan* (the pheasant-feather headpiece), he attends to the Emperor’s consultations and presides over the attendants, always remaining by the sovereign’s side.
As for Yiyang County, its prefecture is located in Hengzhou. "Founding a state" (*kaiguo*) means establishing the altars of soil and grain for the Emperor. "Marquis" (*hou*) means to wait;
it refers to acting as an outpost for the Son of Heaven against any irregularities. Among the five ranks of nobility, this corresponds to the second. The fief...
Four hundred *li* were established as his fief.

His mother, Lady Xu, was gentle, kind, respectful, and frugal; she was particularly diligent in her observance of fasts and purifications. She dreamed that five-colored fragrant smoke floated lightly like a mist.
It lingered in his mind, and he wished to brush it away. He heard a voice say: "The karmic conditions of past lives have entrusted you to the Way of Kings;
merit and virtue will come of their own accord, so why would you cast them off?"
At birth, his eyes possessed double pupils, resembling the physiognomic marks of Shun.
Furthermore, he dreamed of swallowing a white rat; upon waking, his body felt heavy.
The stele at Jingzhou states: "His mother then felt her body and mind become like empty space. Finding this strange, she divined the matter on that day."
He then said, "The white mouse was a transformation of a dragon.
Upon his birth, a divine light appeared at night; the halls and buildings were brilliantly illuminated, casting radiance even upon the neighboring houses."
That year was the fifth year of the Datong era of the Liang dynasty. An inscription at a stele in Jingzhou states:
"One day at dusk, the villagers saw fire break out from atop a house. Its flames rose up on all sides, and the entire community came to extinguish it.
Upon arrival, they found that a child had been born in the home of the Attendant-in-Ordinary Chen; everyone was struck with wonder."

The neighbors remembered the auspicious omens of his past and called him Wangdao (Royal Way); later, based on his subsequent physical marks, they further named him Guangdao (Radiant Way), thus establishing these two characters for him.
His eyes possessed double pupils; though his parents concealed and protected this trait, wishing it not to be known by others, people nonetheless knew of it themselves.

The *Nanshan zhuan* states: On the night of his birth, the interior of the room was brilliantly illuminated. This light ceased after two nights and two days. Those both inside and outside were filled with joy;
they all set out sacrificial vessels and offerings to celebrate together. They believed that if the fire had been extinguished and the water cold, the matter would not have been accomplished.
Suddenly, two monks came and knocked on the door, saying, "Excellent! One with the virtue of a ghost must surely leave the household life. Having spoken, they vanished.
The *Jingbei* states that while in his swaddling clothes, he would spontaneously join his palms. Although these accounts differ in wording, their meaning is the same.
As for what he did not wish others to know: that his eyes possessed double pupils is the mark of Emperor Shun; he feared [it would be revealed].

Because he was being harmed [by his parents], when he reached the age of seven, he delighted in going to the monastery. The monks orally transmitted the "Universal Gate" chapter (*Samantamukha-parivarta*) to him; upon hearing it for the first time, he mastered it immediately.
However, his parents forbade him and would not allow him to go there frequently.

The Jingbei states: While still in his childhood, monks recognized his spiritual capacity (*indriya*). They orally transmitted to him the "Universal Gate Chapter" (*Samantamukha-parivarta*) of the Lotus Sūtra;
upon hearing it once, he mastered the entire scroll and could recite it fluently from memory. The assembly all marveled at this. *E* means to stop; *ting* means to permit.
This implies that he was not permitted to frequent the monastery (*vihāra*) excessively. *Zhaochen* refers to the age of losing one's teeth; for a boy, this occurs at eight years of age.
"Girls lose their teeth at seven years of age; this is because the Yin is swift while the Yang is slow.
Whenever he reflected on the principles he had recited, he felt sorrowful that he had not heard [the full text].
'Sorrowful' (chóuchàng) means to feel regret and resentment. When Kumārajīva was translating the *Lotus Sūtra*, he lost one verse from the 'Universal Gateway' chapter."
The verses were translated during the Sui dynasty by Jñānagupta. It was not until the Tang dynasty that they were finally incorporated into the great compendium by the masters of the Nanshan school.
Consequently, there are many who lament that they were unable to hear the verses in their entirety.
Suddenly and spontaneously, he mastered the remaining passages and sentences. Later, upon verification, there was nothing lost.
"Mastering the remaining passages and sentences" refers to either the verses or the entire text.
The people of his village sighed in wonder at his extraordinary nature. Is this not what is meant by "warming the old to know the new"?
As for "village" (xiāng), according to ancient regulations, two thousand five hundred households constituted a *xiāng*. A "neighborhood gate" (*lǚ*) refers to the entrance of such a village.
From birth, he was exceptional; even as a child, he was intelligent and brilliant. Everyone sighed in wonder at him. The phrase "warming the old" and so forth originates from [the Analects].
The *Analects* states: "One who warms over the old and knows the new can serve as a teacher.
Yet, regarding the virtue of a Great Master—one who is born with innate knowledge—he reached the age of fifteen, the time for formal study, just as the reign of Emperor Xiaoyuan met with defeat.
Hou Jing falsely established [his own authority]. Emperor Jianwen changed the Taiching era to the first year of the Dabao era.
Emperor Yuan, knowing that Jianwen’s power was held by a treacherous minister and could not be utilized, peacefully changed the era name at Jiangling to the first year of the Chengsheng era.
By the third year, in the eleventh month, his state fell; he was captured by the Wei. On the *xinchou* day of the twelfth month, the Wei people murdered him.
Emperor, your house and state have suffered total ruin; your kinsmen have been exiled.
At the end of the Liang dynasty’s fortune, the nation perished and the royal kin were lost; the family was destroyed and its members scattered. Of those who remain, there are but a few.
I sigh that glorious meetings are difficult to endure for long and lament that withering separation easily arrives.
The nature of circumstances is impermanent; it is like the cluster of flowers meeting the spring dew: the many petals vie for their fragrance, yet they encounter [the rain].

Because of the wind and rain, the withered red petals lie scattered upon the ground, making their fading all too visible; it may be said that the decline of the times and circumstances is easily reached.
Before a statue in Changsha, he made a vast and great vow, swearing to become a śramaṇa and to shoulder the burden of the True Dharma as his own primary responsibility.
Ren. Changsha refers to the administrative seat of Changsha Commandery in Tanzhou, located in the southern route of Jingzhou.

As for that commandery, there was a very long sandbank in the middle of the river; hence it was called Changsha. Within the monastery of that state, before the Buddha image, during the [Liu] Song dynasty...
I do not yet know what name this imperial court uses for this monastery. However, the Great Master was born in Jingzhou, which belonged to the Jinghu North Road;
it is now Jangling, and has further been changed to Jingmen Commandery.

Moreover, since the Great Master was young and the journey was far, he likely went specifically to pay his respects because there were particularly sublime [sites] there. Hong is also from Yang. As for the vow—
This is the regulation. One should manifest the great vows to self-restrain the mind through the Four Great Vows. *Śramaṇa* translates as "diligent and quiescent":

being diligent in cultivating wholesome fruits and quiescent in ceasing all unwholesome conduct. To carry on the shoulders is called "bearing" (*he*), while to hold upon the back is called "carrying" (*fu*).
As his sincerity had moved the divine response, he dreamed that the auspicious image flew down to his courtyard and extended its golden hand through a window opening to stroke his head three times.
Thereupon, he grew deeply weary of the prison of the household and resolved to extinguish the root of suffering.
The "Auspicious Image" (Ruixiang) refers to the Buddha of Changsha. "Gong" (隙) means a lattice window.

Those who are profoundly weary of the prison of the household life—according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, "Living at home is like being bound in a prison; leaving the home life is like being open and vast as space"—therefore sighed, saying that the body is the root of suffering.
However, out of parental affection, my parents did not grant me permission at the proper time.
What was previously stated—that my parents obstructed me and would not allow me to go frequently—refers precisely to this.
Although I merely complied with their wishes, my sleep and nourishment remained uneasy.
"Wei" and "wei" are identical; "wei" is a respectful response to "nuo. The *Qu li* states: "When the father summons, one does not respond with 'nuo';
one responds with 'wei' and rises to listen. This is because one dares not oppose him; it is an act of compliance. "Qin" means to sleep; "bu" means to eat.
Yet, when the mind is enslaved by leaving the household, one's sleep and food become unsettled.

He then carved sandalwood to create a statue and consulted the scriptures within the Tripiṭaka. Morning and night he performed prostrations and recited the texts, his mindfulness continuing without interruption.
"Carving sandalwood" refers to sculpting a statue; "copying an image" refers to painting one. Facing the statue, he prostrated; holding the scripture, he practiced its recitation.

When prostrating before the Buddha, his entire body fell to the ground; he was as if in a dream, seeing a most lofty mountain overlooking a vast ocean, its waters clear and still, its vegetation lush and dense, each reflecting the other in mutual brilliance.
"Huang" (恍) means "hazy and indistinct," like the state of one entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*). It is vividly clear yet resembles a dream.

As for the "lofty mountain," this refers to when the Great Master later returned to Tiantai and held a ceremony for releasing living beings; from his boat at the mouth of the sea, he gazed upon the beautiful mountain.
His former dream of wandering by the seashore was precisely like this. Examining it against the Jing stele, it is understood to have been a dream after he had received full ordination as a monk.
Now, Zhan’an says this refers to a dream he had before leaving home, whereas the *Biographies of Nanshan* states that it was a dream he had while residing at Waguan Temple;
there are thus differences between these accounts.

At the summit of the mountain was a monk who clapped his hands and called for [the traveler] to ascend; in an instant, he extended his arm to the foot of the mountain, leading him up to enter a monastery.
There, he saw the statues he had commissioned inside the temple hall.
The monk was none other than Dīpaṃkara himself. There remains at that site a stone used for clapping one's hands.
The monastery is the former Xuchansi, now known as Daci Monastery. The vision seen later manifested itself before him.
As for the images he saw being fashioned, these were the carvings and painted portraits mentioned previously. That which was seen within the dream was the result of his profound sincerity.

In a dream, he wept and set forth his aspiration: "I vow that upon attaining the Buddha-dharma of the three periods of time, I shall expound it without impediment before a thousand masters of the śāstras.
In the Western Land, Vasubandhu initially studied the Hīnayāna and did not believe in the Mahāyāna teachings; he composed five hundred treatises.
He continued to advocate for the Hīnayāna. Later, however, due to the guidance of his elder brother Asaṅga, he came to realize the meaning of the Mahāyāna.

He then took up a blade, intending to cut out his own tongue as an act of repentance; but Asaṅga stopped him, saying, "In the past you used this tongue to disparage [the Mahāyāna], and now you use this tongue to praise it."
It was sufficient. Thereupon, he further composed five hundred treatises in praise and exposition of the Mahāyāna; at that time, he was known as the "Master of a Thousand Treatises.
Zhiyi vowed: "Should I encounter such a person of vast talent and profound erudition, I would also respond to him without hesitation."
How much less, then, could those who are but single wheels or solitary wings— such as the eminent masters of Jinling like Jì and Rěn—
be worthy of inquiring into the depths of the Great Master’s treasury? Thus,
may the four worldly requisites not have been bestowed upon them in vain.
"Empty" refers to the Tang dynasty. The "four matters" are food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine.
The monk Shenbi raised his hand toward the image and spoke again, saying: "You shall dwell here; you shall pass away here."
After the Great Master dispersed his assembly in Jiangnan and first returned to Tiantai, he finally met Dingguang to recount the matter of his dream;
what is recorded in the following text is extremely clear.
Having awakened from sleep, he saw that his own body was prostrate before the Buddha; the tears shed in his dream had fallen to the ground and formed a stream.
With grief and joy mingling in his heart, his diligent application became even more intense.
"Wu" means to awaken. "Like a flowing stream" refers to tears falling profusely like the flow of water.
"Sorrow and joy" means sorrowing that worldly beings do not see [the Buddha] and rejoicing that one has personally attained the vision. "Yu" means to surpass; "zhi" means extreme.
Later, he encountered the untimely death of his two parents and suffered the bitter agony of mourning.

This section differs from that on the Jing stele; while the latter states that he sought to leave the household life while his parents were still living, this text says he departed from secular life after the passing of both parents.
The Jing stele further records: "The Six Teachers wished to take up their staffs and travel everywhere to view the magnificent sights of various regions."
He took leave of his mother. His mother said, "My son, you are now traveling far away; on whom shall your parents rely for sweet delicacies?

There was Yuan Zixiong of Chenjun, who fled to Linbaili; and there was also Yu Chong of Xinye, who collected taxes from the people in three installments.

Both men went up a mountain where they encountered a lecture on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*. Consequently, they observed the fast for several days, listening to the Dharma with single-minded devotion.

Zixiong saw before the hall a mountain whose lapis lazuli surface was transparent and clear. On the shaded side of the mountain, a winding stream had beryl strewn across its bed, spanned by a rainbow bridge and filled with...

Adorned with precious ornaments, dozens of Indian monks emerged from the mountain, each holding an incense burner in his hand. As they ascended the bridge and entered the hall, their majestic deportment filled the eyes and the fragrance of the incense reached the nostrils.
Daorong informed Huichong of this, but Huichong claimed he had seen nothing; their fates were thus as divergent as heaven and earth, for it was Daorong who perceived it.
Consequently, Daorong resolved to rebuild the lecture hall. This event was not long ago, and the hall remains there even today.
Xinye. This is the name of a commandery; it originally belonged to Jingzhou. After the Jin Emperor Wu pacified the Wu kingdom, he established Xinye Commandery.
Regarding the "three levies" (sanke): they are not seen in any extant texts. Some say they consist of money, cloth, silk, grain, and rice, but this cannot yet be accepted as authoritative.
Since the three levies collected by Lord Yu from the people were merely a crude tax, they should have been paid to the government; why then would they be used for acts of renunciation and giving?
It is feared that at that time the imperial decree permitted it; since it was not his own property, it would instead have become a disturbance to the people.
This is why the Sage did not allow him to see it. The "Hall" refers to the lecture hall of Daci.

However, Mount Tiantai presses down upon the vast ocean. The common people there rely on fishing for their livelihood. Those who build bridges cut off the mountain streams; those who establish embankments dam the sea.
When the autumn waters rise, both large and small fish fill the bridges; with the twice-daily tides, the waves roar and surge against the dykes. Skulls form mountains and flies swarm like thunder;
it is not only the creatures of water and land that are pitiable, but one also grieves for the countless deaths of boatmen. Previously...
Out of universal compassion for this purpose, the Master donated his own robes along with various offerings from supporters to redeem a plot of land,
establishing it forever as a pond for the release of living beings.
Taiwan, Haimen, Ninghai, Ming’s Xiangguo, and Wenzhou’s Leshui all border the great ocean to the east.
Regarding the character for "fisherman" (漁), it is composed of "water" (氵); all characters for fisherman employ this radical, as they catch fish within the water.
"Liáng" (梁) refers to the fishing gear used to catch fish. "Zhú" (竺)—the "zhú" being a modification of "zhù" (住)—means "to protect. It refers to using arrows and binding them with ropes and chains.
It is like the image of a screen or a cage. This is because it is a coastal region for fishing and salt production. "Kǒu" refers to the skull; "yǔn" means death.
If a person maintains the pure precepts, they will surely be reborn in the celestial palaces of the Pure Land.
Since killing and injury are grave offenses, one will inevitably fall into the hells. How painful this is!

At that time, Shi Xu was serving as the governor of the commandery. He invited [Seng]ji to lecture on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. His salvation of sentient beings was impartial; he was like a treasure emerging from its cave.

Cultivating his person through compassion, those who saw him were filled with joy. Cultivating his speech through compassion, those who heard his voice would resolve their minds [on enlightenment]. He was diligent and earnest in his skillful guidance.

He guided them toward the law of cause and effect. Consequently, the fishermen along the entire stretch of the region reformed their ways and followed the good; they cherished life and abandoned killing.

For more than three hundred li, where the rapids and tides flow continuously, there were sixty-three fish-traps spanning the rivers and streams, all of which were simultaneously and forever relinquished to become pools of Dharma.
In a single day, the number of lives saved reached hundreds of millions—how could it have been merely ten thousand? Boats were moored side by side upon the river.
He lectured on the "Flowing Water" chapter. Furthermore, he scattered non-glutinous rice as both material and Dharma offerings. As the ship emerged from the sea mouth, they gazed upon Mount Fuyong;
its steep peaks rose up in dense clusters like red lotuses just beginning to bloom, while solitary boulders hung overhangs like withered flowers about to fall.
The Master said, "In the past, I dreamed of wandering by the seashore; it was exactly like this."
The *Bai lu* (Record of a Hundred Matters) states in the "Stele on the Release of Living Creatures":
Ji Shang'er, General of Fierce Proclamation and Interior Historian of Linhai, a descendant of Ji Xun, requested that one copy of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* be preached.

Chen Sizhan, former General of Cloud Cavalry and Interior Historian of Linhai, along with his son Chen Anqing, requested that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* be preached. Shang'er exhorted the local chief (*zhuzhu*).
Yanjùzǔ, Yánggōng Hè, and others together donated sixty-three [temples] at Zhūliáng. The current mention of Jìxǔ likely refers to his name or its phonetic equivalent.
As for the statement "how could it stop at ten thousand," this present act of releasing living beings exceeds the number saved by the Elder Śrotadhara.
Regarding the statement "furthermore, scattering non-glutinous rice," this is also like what Śrotadhara had his son do.
"Renting an elephant" refers to taking the means for drinking and eating from one's home and scattering them into the pond; thus, the food has been joined with the water.
"A pair of boats" means two boats side by side. The dream experienced in the past refers to the dream one had while prostrating before the Buddha at home.
That the boat is now emerging from the sea mouth is a vision that perfectly accords with the omens of that former dream.
The śramaṇa Huìchéng and the District Magistrate Qián Xuánzhì both composed writings in praise of him; these are omitted here due to their length.
At that time, many monastics and laymen of refined literary talent, having witnessed such rare events, produced numerous verses of eulogy.
He first entered Tiantai Mountain and resided there for nine years. The biography merely records that he met Dìngguāng at Huádǐng Peak and heard the *Dhūta* lectures.
Regarding matters such as Jingming’s release of living beings and so forth, this biography records only the events concerning Jizhi and the imperial decree issued to Juqiong.
However, there are four versions of the transmission; in general, this biography is extremely brief. What a pity that it has not been heard of!

Later, Xu returned to the capital. On a separate occasion, he was implicated in other matters and consequently detained along with Yan Wei. As they were about to undergo execution, [Xu] thought of his former teacher and wished for him to provide a rescue.
That night, he dreamed of a multitude of fish, numbering in the billions beyond measure, all spitting foam and soaking him.
The next morning, when Xu descended [from his seat], the Emperor issued a decree specifically pardoning Xu’s crime.
As for calculating the official’s crime, its underlying cause has not yet been seen. "Yan" refers to the current Judicial Official (*sīlǐ guān*).

Regarding "Wèi," the *Hàn Bǎiguān Zhì* states that this office exists among all military officials. Regarding "Yuán," it means to examine the root source (*gēnyuán*) of the crime to establish its credibility.
Those whose offenses were incompatible [with the Dharma] all abandoned him.
At noon, auspicious clouds suddenly arose—yellow, purple, crimson, and white, shaped like lunar halos—condensing in the void and stretching far over the summit of the monastery.
Furthermore, flocks of yellow sparrows flew about, chirping and fluttering noisily, as they settled upon the eaves and roofs for half a day.

The fish departed. The Master said, "The river fish have transformed into yellow sparrows and come here to express their gratitude. The Master dispatched his disciple Huibai to the capital to inform the throne.
Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty issued an imperial edict stating: "Strictly prohibit fishing and hunting; let this place forever be a pond for the release of living beings."

At the end of the hundredth record, Xu Ling’s letter states: "Ling bows respectfully. Regarding the release of living beings, I have heard that your household is most diligent in this auspicious matter;
this is truly a source of joy for me. I have carefully prepared these words and shall not trouble you further with inquiries regarding the Patriarchs.
Furthermore, he sent a letter to the local commander, Xie Ba, stating: "I hereby reiterate this matter as previously presented. An imperial edict stated: "If there were no crows on this river..."

[It is] a rare delicacy. One should comply with the request so that it may forever serve as a pool of merit. It was for fear that Emperor Xuan might enjoy eating this thing and consider it a rare delicacy that these words were spoken.
Prince Chen asked Xu Ling, "Who composed the inscription for the memorial stele of Tiantai? He replied, "I wished that Your Majesty’s divine brush might inscribe it upon jade.
However, the Emperor Xuan passed away, and it could no longer be completed. An imperial decree was issued for Xu Xiaojun, the Director of the National University, to erect a tall stele.
The stele stands on the mountain to this day; those who behold it shed tears.

The Eastern Palace is also called the Spring Palace. The Crown Prince resides in the Eastern Palace just as the spring qi begins to arise, nurturing his sagely virtue like a tree spreading its branches to provide shade and benefit for the people.
This was Chen Houzhu, whose name was Shubao and whose courtesy name was Yuanshou.
In the fourteenth year of Taian, Emperor Xuan passed away; he ascended the throne and changed the era name to Zhide, the first year.
In the first month of the fourth year, the era name was changed to Zhengming. During his reign, he was dissolute and negligent, leading to the destruction of his state by the Sui dynasty.
A stele erected by Xu Xiaokē stands at Guoqing Temple; when people see the stele, they recall his compassionate governance and shed tears for him.
When Prince Yongyang, the Crown Prince Chen Wenhuang, went to govern the regions of Ou and Yue, he repeatedly sent earnest letters of invitation.

He subsequently traveled to Yuyue and personally practiced the Vaipulya (fangdeng) teachings. His kinsmen and retinue likewise received the pure precepts; they engaged in lectures and exegesis by day and practiced seated meditation by night.
The king’s name was Bozhi (伯智), his courtesy name being Cezhi (策之). He was the eighth son of Emperor Wen of the Chen dynasty.
His biography is recorded in the fifty-fifth fascicle of the *Nanshi* (南史), though it is extremely brief, stating only that he was widely versed in the classics and histories;

during the Taian era, he was promoted to Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (*shangshu zuopuye*), and later became a Special Advancement (*tejin*). After the fall of the Chen, he entered Chang’an and served as the Director of the National Academy (*guozisiye*) under the Sui dynasty.
The *Nanshan Zhuan* states that when he was dispatched to govern Wuxing, he requested the Great Master to bestow the precepts upon him. During the Chen and Sui dynasties, Tai was called Guazhou;
it was within the territory of Ouyue. Alternatively, it is said that during the reign of Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty, he was dispatched as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Dongzhou;
hence it is said that he was "dispatched to govern Ouyue."

The former master said to his disciple Zhiyue, "I wish to exhort the King to cultivate merit and avert calamity; would this be appropriate? Zhiyue replied, "The court officials have no long-standing ties with you;
they will surely speak of your coldness and heat [of character]. The master said, "To quell the world's censure and suspicion is itself a virtuous act.

Later, when the King went out on an excursion, he fell from his horse and was nearly killed. Zhiyue was then moved by remorse and felt grief-stricken with shame and regret. The former master personally took him as his teacher.
The assembly performed the Avalokiteśvara Repentance Rite with focused minds and single-minded devotion. The King’s consciousness cleared slightly, and he sat leaning against his desk.
Seeing this, a Brahman monk holding an incense burner stepped directly forward and asked the King, "How is your illness? The King, dripping with sweat, could not answer.
The monk then circumambulated the king once. Fragrance wafted about, and as he turned to the right, he suddenly felt his agonizing pain completely released.
First, the precepts and wisdom had purified his mind; now, this spiritual efficacy further gladdened his eyes. How could one who does not wish to believe possibly avoid being moved?
Zhìyuè was a preeminent disciple of Zhìzhě. His religious practices and cultivation of dhyāna are recorded within his biography.

The Patriarch, knowing through spiritual insight that the King was about to meet with calamity, wished to perform rites to avert it. However, because Zhìyuè was not among the long-standing attendants of the King, the King’s aides suspected that the monk intended to seek some personal gain.
Consequently, they subjected him to harsh and cold insults. [The Patriarch] therefore followed their counsel, and [the King] was thus spared.

This led to public censure and suspicion. His *Pranidhāna* (Vow Text) states: "I look up with reverence to the Upādhyāya of Tiantai. His virtue equals that of Dao’an and Huiyuan; his Way surpasses that of Fotudeng and Daoyou. Far and near, all incline their hearts toward him;
as he raises his staff, the faithful gather like clouds. He succeeds the declining Dharma of the Semblance Age to rescue those in ignorance and delusion, manifesting the Sun of Wisdom."
The double brilliance [of your virtue] is employed to rescue the decadent customs of the age. Furthermore, you roam through the Dharma, penetrating the depths of Chan.

The fetters of conditioned existence have already been severed, and the patience of non-arising has manifested before you. As for your disciples, we are tossed by the winds of karma and submerged in the waters of craving;

though we partake of the joy of the Dharma, we cannot dispel our clouded and obscured minds. We merely look up to the bliss of Chan, yet in the end harbor a mind of distraction and agitation. [Like] the sun’s orb...
The reins of the sun and moon gallop on without ceasing; the shadow of Chang’e in her lunar chariot is difficult to detain.
There is parting and there is meeting—what words can express this sighing? Cherishing the Dharma and revering the Dharma, my devotion flows on without end.
May I, in birth after birth, encounter Master Tiantai, constantly making offerings to him, just as Zhiji served Jizheng Tathāgata, or as Bhaiṣajyarāja beheld [the Buddha].
The Perfectly Enlightened One of Thunderous Sound [resides in] An-yang and Tuṣita; both are unified within the One Vehicle.
The current text transmits only one hundred and sixty-eight characters, whereas the *Bai lu* (Hundred Records) contains seven hundred and forty-six characters;
the present text is thus abbreviated. Regarding the phrase "wandering," "you" (wandering) refers to the free movement of a blade, like the butcher Ding dissecting an ox. Day after day...
"Whole ox" (quán niú) refers to the surging waves; it is like the vast and boundless great ocean with its massive billows.

"Conditioned fetters" (*saṃyojana*) refer to the views and afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms. Although the Great Master’s rank was at the fifth stage, he truly spoke of these conditioned fetters.
This is as Liang Su praised him: "The stages of Equal Enlightenment and Wondrous Enlightenment are such that they cannot be known. "To gallop" means to run.
Furthermore, Xihe was the minister of Yao who oversaw the sun; he was thus named after his office. "Reins" refers to the halter ropes of a horse.
This expresses the sentiment that time passes as swiftly as an arrow, and one regrets not being able to seize the reins of the sun’s chariot to hold it back.
Chang’e is the mistress of the lunar palace; in Buddhism, she is called the Moon Palace Deva King. External teachings (non-Buddhist traditions) associate the moon with yin.
Therefore it is said that Chang’e possesses a magnificent countenance. Her shadow is difficult to detain; her reins do not pause—these two meanings are one and the same.
"Chányuán" describes the appearance of flowing water, serving as a metaphor for tears falling uncontrollably.
As for "Ji-zhì," he is the eldest of the sixteen princes, whose name is Ji-zhì. "Yào" [refers to]...

"King who beholds the Thunderous Sound" (Wáng jìn léiyīn zhě) is a passage from the "Chapter on King Wondrous Adornment" (Miàozhuāngyánwáng pǐn). Regarding "sweeping away the Three Vehicles" (dàng yīshèng):

the *Bǎilù* states that whether one is born in the World of Ultimate Bliss or dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, in both cases one sweeps away the practices of the Three Vehicles and turns toward the Path of the One Vehicle.
The present text provides only a brief excerpt.

Although our former teacher harbored his treasures in a remote valley, his fame resounded throughout the capital; though he concealed his form in a secluded ravine, his virtuous kindness was brilliantly manifest.
The profound meditation of the Great Way was stored within his inner heart. His person was hidden in deep valleys like a black pearl or Jingle jade;
though concealed within his breast, the world already knew him—his brilliance was clear and his presence was fully revealed.
The young Emperor Chen consulted his ministers, asking, "Who among those of the Buddhist community is most eminent?

Xu Ling replied, "The Chan Master of Waguan Monastery possesses virtue that surpasses wind and frost, and his insight into meditation is as deep as the ocean. In the past, when he traveled to the capital, he was revered by the multitude of worthies;

now, as he dwells in lofty retreat at Tiantai, the clouds of the Dharma spread across the east. Prince Yongyang has personally received his teachings from the north. I pray that Your Majesty will issue an edict for him to return."

He propagated the Dharma throughout the realm, causing both monastics and laypeople to receive its benefits. At the beginning, the Chen ruler first dispatched his attendant Zhao Junqing; he sent Zhu Lei, the Chief Scribe, a second time;
and for the third time, he dispatched an imperial edict. He subsequently sent the monk Fasheng, all of whom were personally addressed with letters written by the Emperor’s own hand.
He consistently feigned illness and was unfit for the task. The Chen ruler consequently appointed three envoys and further issued an edict to the prefecture to earnestly entreat him.

According to the *Nanshan zhuan*, seven such envoys were dispatched in succession, all with personal letters from the Emperor’s own hand; the current text mentions three envoys who were ordered to the prefecture.
Thus, Prince Yongyang was appointed to govern Ou-yue (Yuezhou). A letter from Prince Yongyang requesting [the Master’s presence] is also recorded in the *Baolu* (Records of the Hundred).

Prince Yongyang submitted this remonstrance: "The Sovereign has humbled himself, and the court is filled with reverence. A single word of benefit would bring relief to the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*).
If you were to retire in high-minded refusal to the deep mountains, compassion would be obstructed. Your disciple is weak and insignificant, yet you have condescended to come."
When asked what his purpose was in going to Taiwan, he replied: "I reflect upon myself and find no virtue; my station has been obscure.

If there is fault, it falls upon me alone—how could I allow others to be unjustly implicated? Karmic conditions are like water: where it rises, it flows away; where it hollows, it remains. My ambition cannot be satisfied; I simply let things take their course."
When one errs, the body must bear the consequences. This is the answer given to Prince Yongyang; it refers to the principle that evil deeds naturally recoil upon oneself.

"Lóng" (隆) means high. "Yǔ" (窳)—pronounced *wǎo*—means low. It is a natural law that water flows toward the low; one cannot stubbornly resist this, but must simply allow things to follow their conditions (*yúan*).
He then departed for Jinling. On the road, he encountered two imperial envoys: first, Huang Jibao, an attendant of the Imperial Secretariat; second, Chen Jianzong, a Chief Scribe.

They invited him to the Eastern Hall, where they provided him with the four types of offerings and treated him with profound courtesy. He established a community of Chan practitioners at Lingyao Temple and expounded the *Śāstra on the Awakening of Faith* at Taiji.
Furthermore, he lectured on the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, with one hundred seats arranged to his left for the five ranks of officials.

He sat to the right. The Chen ruler personally attended the banquet to listen to the Dharma. The Monastic Rectifier Huìgěng, the Monastic Superintendent Huìkuàng, and Huìbiàn of Chánggān all received imperial edicts to engage in debate.
It was as if towering winter ice were being simultaneously bound and dissolved, or like the scorching heat of summer that can melt it away.
The Son of Heaven was delighted, and the hundred officials paid their full respects.

The five ranks are Duke, Marquis, Earl, Viscount, and Baron. Since Buddhism came to the East, successive sovereigns have listened to the Dharma; these instances are extensively recorded in the *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha).
Regarding [Master] Kuṅ (pronounced Guàn), there is no account in the *Sengshi*. His clan and surname are unknown. The *Sengshilüe* (Abridged History of the Sangha) states:

Regarding the term "Sengzheng" (Monastic Rectifier): "Zheng" means "rectitude. It refers to one who rectifies himself and rectifies others, thereby effectively disseminating the correct ordinances; hence the name.
During the Song dynasty, the position of "Shamen Du" (Metropolitan of the Śramaṇas) was established; this is what is now called "Sengdu" (Monastic Metropolitan).

When the lecture concluded, Huìkēng held up an incense burner before the seat of honor and said: "The state has held more than ten fasting assemblies, and I have personally presided over four lectures.
I have analyzed the texts and dissected the principles, believing I had found the true gateway. Yet today, as the stars emerge and gather, I see my own cleverness and recognize my shortcomings.

While disputes and competitions have never ceased in the past, this assembly is characterized by profound solemnity; for seven nights it has been tranquil and still, with a thousand branches of flowers shining in splendor—all through the power of the Dharma King."

Furthermore, when the Prince of Chen offered his thanks at Guangde Hall, he said: "Not only do I look up to and entrust myself to the Buddha-dharma, but I also wish to acknowledge my own many shortcomings.
Although Sengxiong analyzed and answered these points, he did not cut off their root source; thus, the Prince continued to offer his words, unable to be restrained. The Great Master’s wisdom...
The ocean’s abyss is profound and wondrous, exhausting the depths of the mysterious and the arcane; thus, he had me search through the lecture texts for seven nights.

My contentious mind was silenced and stilled, becoming tranquil and serene—like spring flowers, a thousand branches blooming in splendor, reflecting the sun upon the eaves. Who would not say this is beautiful?
"Wei" (委) means to entrust; "ji" (及) means to reach. It is not only that the Buddha-dharma is entrusted to the Great Master, but the State also has [something]...
As for those who have not yet attained [the Way], I also hope that you will deign to provide words of instruction to guide them; thus, I offer this prayer.

Among the monks and nuns examined by the state in the present age, there are ten thousand who lack official registration. According to the deliberations of the court, those whose conduct does not accord with the scriptures must cease their religious practice.
The former master admonished him, saying: "Tishya recited ten thousand words daily yet could not avoid hell; Pūrṇa recited but a single verse and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
In earnest discussion, it is the Way alone that matters; how can it depend upon reciting much? The Prince of Chen was greatly pleased and immediately halted the selection process.

"Those without a thread" (wúguànzhě): "thread" (guàn) means to pierce through. It refers to those who lack the guiding principle by which they are sustained, like oxen and horses in the wild that have lost their guiding lines and the flow of their paths.
Devadatta is also called Tiépódáduō; this translates as "one whose heart is feverish with human pride."
He was the younger brother of the Buddha and the eldest son of King Śuklodana. His height was one *zhang*, five *chi*, and four *cun*.
Having left the household life, he attained the four *dhyāna* concentrations and possessed supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). His faculties were sharp; he could recite ten thousand words a day.

In contrast, Upāli’s faculties were dull, and he could only recite half a verse. The verse says: "Guard the mouth, restrain the mind, and let not the body transgress; by doing so, one realizes Arhatship."
[The previous record] says "Fruit" (Guo), but now it says "One Practice" (Yixing);
I fear this is an error. However, his dwelling at Lingyao was excessively cramped; seeking a more secluded and tranquil place, he established a community for the practice of dhyāna.

Suddenly, he dreamed of a man with a solemn and orderly retinue who called himself Guanda and invited him to reside at Sanqiao. The Master said, "Guanda" was the Dharma-name of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty.

"Sanqiao—could this not be Guangzhai? he thought, and so he moved his residence there. In the fourth month of that year, the Emperor of Chen visited the temple and performed a "giving of the body" (sheshen) great almsgiving.

He also lectured on the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. As soon as the introductory discourse was finished, the Emperor rose from within the great assembly and prostrated three times, bowing with profound earnestness to manifest his deep respect.
From the Crown Prince downward, all relied upon him as their vessel for salvation, and they all followed his teachings.

He held the precepts as his model to serve as a lofty guide. His former teacher, having emptied himself and abandoned all reception, was able to remain at peace amidst honor and disgrace; thus, when discussing the non-existent, he showed no surprise or alarm.
When Emperor Wu of Liang entered Tongtai Temple to offer his body as a great gift of almsgiving, the court ministers offered hundreds of millions of strings of cash to redeem him.
The Emperor-Bodhisattva and the monastic assembly gave their silent consent. The Prince of Chen subsequently emulated this practice;
thus it is called the "Great Gift of Relinquishing the Body. From the Crown Prince downward, all the palace ladies, consorts, and princes received the precepts.
Later, Empress Shen, the consort of the Sovereign, wrote a letter requesting a dharma-name, which was titled Haihui Bodhisattva (Ocean Wisdom Bodhisattva). Zhangan [Zhiyi] omitted this detail.
This is a scriptural teaching. The precepts are likened to a life-preserving float that enables one to cross the ocean of suffering; the metaphor of the ship and the ferry is likewise intended.
"Ferry" (*jin*) refers to water; "path" (*dao*) refers to guidance. Since the ocean of suffering is difficult to cross, one must rely on the precepts as a guide.
The Petition for Precepts by the Crown Prince states: Yuan bows in homage. Looking up, I reflect that the Way of transformation is without fixed method;

it saves sentient beings according to their capacities, protects the land, and draws in those of the heavens and the human realm. Its illumination is brilliant and radiant, and it entrusts its traces to teachers and friends. When the Bhikṣu entered my dream, I was moved.

The image of the tally-token has long been manifest; now the Venerable Jiaozhang has arrived in person. The virtue of the high seat is thus upheld. Therefore, our hearts reach out toward the Ten Stages, and we thirst for and look up to the Four Reliances.
Regarding the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as the two teachings of inner and outer, honoring the teacher and revering the Way have been traditions since time immemorial.
We humbly hope that you will deign to grant us your guidance and comply with our request, so that we may form karmic bonds life after life and fulfill our great vow, day and night.
[His merit] increased. On the fifth day of the second month, a Dharma assembly for a thousand monks was established at Chongzheng Hall.

[The Emperor] respectfully invited him to serve as the Preceptor for Bodhisattva Precepts and dispatched the Chief Scribe Liu Xuan to welcome him (and so forth). At that time, as he passed the incense in his hand, tears flowed down his cheeks.
Since his name was written as Shanmeng (Good Sprout), it was now too late for its fulfillment. Later, when the Great Sui swallowed the Chen dynasty, he finally realized [the meaning].
Regarding the previous point:
according to the *Nanshi* (History of the Southern Dynasties), Annals, the name of the Later Emperor’s crown prince was Shen; it is an error to say his name was Yuan.
When the Sui dynasty annexed Chen, he was fifteen years old and sat within his closed chambers, attended by the palace attendant Kong Boyu, while armored soldiers knocked [at the gate].
He entered through the side door. [Hui]shen sat deeply composed and comforted him, saying, "For soldiers on the road, you have not reached a state of exhaustion.
On the *jisi* day of the third month in the third year of the Zhengming era, he entered Chang’an with his father, the King, and his kinsmen; after this, nothing further was known of his end.

When the bhikṣu entered the dream, it was precisely at the time of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding the character for his name, *Bǐng*, the *Nánshān Zhì* (Biographies from the Southern Mountains) writes it as *Bìng*.

"Bǐng" means to hold; "bǐng" means to illuminate. One should use the character "bǐng" from the latter [group]. Regarding the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Grounds, they are fully recorded in the numerical categories (*fashù*).

As for the Four Reliances (*sìyī*), Mount Gushan’s verse states: "The five grades and the ten faiths constitute the first two; the practices (*xíng*) and the directions (*xiàng*) constitute the third;
Equal Enlightenment (*děngjué*) and Sublime Enlightenment (*miàojiào*) are the fourth. The Great Master is thus the first reliance. His ordination name was Shàn Méng.
This refers to when a sprout first emerges but has not yet formed its trunk. In the second year of the Zhengming era, he received the precepts; in the third year, the state was destroyed.

Having been designated to the position of Crown Prince, his "trunk" had not yet been formed. Later, when the matter was investigated, it perfectly corresponded to the initial meaning of the term "sprout.

Thus, it is said: "Only then did he realize the former intent. Emperor Wen of Sui, whose name was Jian, received the abdication from the Zhou dynasty and dispatched Prince Jin, Yang Guang, as [his successor].
The Marshal appointed He Ruo-bi as his deputy general to swallow Chen. Sui originally had no "running";
once it returned to the Tang state, only after its departure was the term "running" added.

After Jinling fell, [Hui]ce took up his staff and traveled through Jing and Xiang. While passing through Bencheng, he suddenly dreamed of an elderly monk who said, "The auspicious image of Tao Kan respectfully requests you to protect it.
Thereupon, he went to rest at Mount Kuang, where he beheld the portrait of Yuan'ong and verified the spiritual power of the Dharma Master from Yanmen.
Shortly thereafter, Xunyang rebelled and the temple buildings were set ablaze; yet, on this mountain alone, the golden [image] remained unharmed.
Regarding the incursions and disturbances, the merit of protecting the sacred image lies precisely here.
Later, the Ruler set out from Jianye for Chang’an together with his hundred officials. Emperor Wen of the Sui temporarily allocated residences in the capital to await him;
both the interior and exterior were thoroughly prepared, and he dispatched envoys to welcome and comfort him. The people of Chen sang songs of praise, forgetting [their former grievances].
He was about to pass away. He sent a messenger back to report: "From the current ruler downward, those great and small on the road for five hundred *li* are continuous without end.
Emperor Wen sighed, saying, "How can it have reached this point? Bamboo is called *ce* (a staff), and wood is called *zhang* (a cane);
here they are used interchangeably. Jingxiang refers to the two prefectures of the Jinghu North Road. Pencheng is also called a *pu* (harbor); it is situated along...
"Pu" refers to present-day Jiangzhou. This old monk was Master Huiyuan; his secular surname was Jia, and he was a native of Yanmen.
As for Tao Kan, the *Book of Jin* states that his courtesy name was Shixing. Originally from Nanyang, when the Jin dynasty conquered Wu, he moved his family to Xunyang in Lujiang.
He rose to the rank of Chancellor (Xiangwei). While Kan served as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Guangzhou, there was a fisherman at sea...

Every evening, Zhibin witnessed the manifestation of divine light and, suspecting it to be a supernatural marvel, reported it to Fan Kan. Kan then dispatched an official to investigate and verify the matter.
Suddenly, a golden image was seen gliding across the waves; the official immediately took it aboard his boat. An inscription on the body of the image read: "The Mañjuśrī Image created by King A.
Kan subsequently sent the image to Hanxi Temple in Wuchang County for veneration. Kan...
Later, he returned to Jingzhou and intended to transport the image on his travels. Previously, the image had been moved by handcart with only a few people required to lift it;
however, when the time came, even after adding several hundred strong men, it remained as immovable as a grindstone. Subsequently, they used ox-carts to pull it until it reached the boat.
The boat sank once more, and the messenger was terrified; he then sent the image back to its original temple.

When Dharma Master Huiyuan completed the construction of Donglin Temple, he held an incense burner toward the direction [of the temple] and prayed for it. The image then floated gracefully through the air and arrived at the site.
The Great Master wished to travel to Jingzhou, relying on the image for protection. "Qiè" means to rest briefly. Kuangshan is also called Lushan. As for the mountain...
Its shape is square; thus it is called Kuāng (Rectangular). The Crown Prince of King Líng of the Zhōu dynasty once built a thatched hut on this mountain.
It is also said that Dōnlín was established by the Dharma Master Huìyuǎn, while Xīlín was established by the Dharma Master Huìqiú;
both sites contain shrines with images [of the masters]. Shortly thereafter, the rebels in Xúnyáng followed [the example of] Shùn in their rebellion.
When factions are divided, it is called rebellion. Although the Sui had pacified Chen, the people of Chen remained unsubdued.
At that time, Li Leng and others gathered a multitude in Jiangnan to rebel; furthermore, Zhu Mojian styled himself the Regional Inspector of Nanxu and occupied Jingkou with his troops.
Furthermore, there were Gu Shiyu and Shen Xuankuai of Jinling; these five locations all suffered great turmoil, which was entirely quelled by the Marshal Yang Su as he led his troops to subdue them.
During the reign of Emperor Wuzong of the Tang, when he destroyed monasteries throughout the empire, a monk hid this image within a mountain valley.
When Emperor Xuanzong restored the Buddhist teachings, the image had vanished and could not be found.

When King Xiaowang of Qin heard of his reputation, he sent an envoy to invite him. The Master addressed the messenger, saying, "Although I wish to meet you, I fear that in the end our conditions will not harmonize.
Subsequently, the king’s officials pressed him with urgency until he could no longer refuse. Just as he was about to cast off his moorings, a great wind suddenly arose.
Within ten days, bandits and rebels rose up in sudden revolt; the waterways and land routes were blocked, and thus the journey could not proceed.
Regarding the King of Qin: among the *Bai lu* (Hundred Records), there are two documents requesting that he reside at Fangdeng Monastery in Anzhou.
Emperor Wen of the Sui had five sons: first, Prince Yong of Fangling; second, Emperor Yang; third, Prince Jun of Qin; fourth, Prince Xiu of Yue; and fifth, Prince Liang of Han.
As for the "wicked rebels," the *Ji* (Annals) of Emperor Yang states that Gao Zhihui and others gathered together in Jiangnan to [rebel].

During the period of disorder, Yang Su was dispatched to subdue the rebel leader Gao Zhihui of Qi Jiang, who styled himself the "Eastern Governor of Yang" and commanded a fleet of a thousand vessels, occupying strategic points. Yang Su devised a plan to pacify him.

In the past, when His Majesty governed the Huaihai region, the ten thousand *li* were cleared and pacified. He admired righteousness and honored the worthy; those who sought refuge in him did so as if returning home.
When he dispatched envoys to invite [the Master], the latter packed his bowl and arrived at the appointed time. The Master said, "I share a profound karmic connection with Your Majesty.
Following the current and with the wind at my back, I have arrived in no time. Thereupon, he received the Bodhisattva precepts from the Master.
The *Shangshu*, in the "Yugong" chapter, states: "Huai and Hai constitute Yangzhou. "Supreme Honored One" (*zhizun*) is a title for the Son of Heaven.
When he first received his precepts, he styled himself Prince of Jin (*Jinwang*). This biography was completed later; therefore, this title is used here.
