The former master first declined on account of his own meager virtue; next, he yielded to eminent monks; finally, he recommended his fellow students. Having been urged three times and unable to evade the request, he then sought four vows.
First: "Though I am fond of studying Chan, my practice does not match the Dharma. As my years draw toward the setting sun, I shall merely occupy this rope bed.

When I beat my breast and reflect upon my heart, I realize it is but a borrowed name. My reputation depends on others, and I loathe hearing my faults exaggerated. I pray that you will not [entrust] the Chan Dharma to me."

First, I have been deceived by others. Second, I was born in a remote frontier and grew up amidst chaos and strife; my person is unrefined by formal education, and my speech is clumsy at social pleasantries.

The profound and mysterious teachings beyond the mundane world have long been beyond my lot, and within the conventional bounds of this realm, I possess nothing worthy of note. Though I wish to exercise self-restraint, I fear in the end that my simple honesty may offend others.
I pray you will not hold me to strict standards of decorum. Third, I humbly desire to transmit the lamp of the Dharma to repay the grace of the Buddha’s teaching.

If one’s physical conduct adheres to the monastic precepts, one should give weight to matters of departure and arrival. If departure and arrival are given too much weight, the transmission of the lamp will be interrupted;

if they are given too little weight, one will incur resentment and reproach. To secure one’s own person is not as good as to propagate the Dharma. I pray that you will permit me to act for the sake of the Dharma, without regarding such matters as being too light or too heavy. (4)

For over thirty years, I have dwelt among water and stone until this became my nature. Now that the royal road is unified and the Buddha-Dharma has flourished once more, I have mistakenly received the broad favor of your grace and transformation.
Internally, I exhaust my withered strength to look up and repay your external protection;

yet if thoughts of mountain retreats arise, I pray you will allow me to pursue my own sustenance so that I may bring my remaining life to its end. Grant these four wishes, O Great King, and then I shall attend to your timely summons.
He then hoped for pure precepts; thus, his sublime vow was granted. Regarding the term "border regions" (*biānbǎo*):
Jingzhou belonged to the north of the Yangtze River and was part of the territory of Wei; hence it was a border region.

It frequently encountered turmoil and disorder, such as the rebellion of Hou Jing against the Liang dynasty and the execution of Emperor Yuan by the Wei. Regarding the phrase "transcendent emptiness and mystery" (*fāngwài xūxuán*): from the Jin dynasty until the Liang, [such teachings] were prevalent.
He studied the works of Zhuangzi and Laozi. Wénzhōngzǐ said, "The 'Vast and Mysterious' (xūxuán) flourished and the Jìn dynasty perished;

this was not the fault of Lǎo Dān. This is precisely that meaning. Regarding "restraint" (zūnjié): the *Lǐjì* says, "Therefore, the gentleman is reverent, restrained, and yielding in order to manifest ritual propriety.
"Zūn" means to advance; "jié" means sequence. It refers to advancing and retreating in accordance with the rules of propriety, where one's coming and going is as if weighted with gravity.

Regarding the "transmission of the lamp" being deficient: because the Master was so venerable and majestic, his disciples found it difficult to approach him; thus, in his engagement with sentient beings, he acted according to their capacities, which is why the formal meaning was lacking.

As for the "imperial path being unified": after the subjugation of Chen, the chariots and books were all made uniform. As for "drinking and feeding": [this refers to the common sustenance of the people].

This refers to what was previously stated: "Pecking at peaks and drinking from mountain streams to fulfill the vows of a lifetime. Regarding "wondrously accepting the vow," it means that Prince Jin granted his request.
The text for the requested precepts states:
"I, the disciple Jì, have inherited the accumulation of goodness and was born into the imperial house. From an early age, I received instruction within the palace; the constant teachings..."

Having been nurtured by early training, one’s fortune and well-being reach their fulfillment. One must awaken to the wondrous mechanism [of reality]; thus, one feels shame for the ruggedness of the minor paths and aspires to the leisurely journey of the Mahāyāna.
One laughs at resting within the illusory city and vows to ferry oneself to the further shore. Among the ten thousand practices of a Bodhisattva, the precepts of goodness come first;
among the tenfold vows of a Bodhisattva, single-minded observance is supreme. This is like constructing a palace, which must first have its foundation; to merely erect the superstructure...

In vain, one could never achieve perfection. The traditions of Confucius, Laozi, and Śākyamuni all rely upon this process of refinement and casting. Were there not these rules and models, who would have anyone to look up to for peace and stability?

Indeed, while the Buddha (Nengren) was originally the Upādhyāya and Mañjuśrī secretly served as the Ācārya, it was nonetheless necessary to rely on human teachers to manifest and transmit the sacred teachings.
From the immediate to the distant, through resonance, the Way is realized. Thus, Sudhana exhausted his very marrow before Samudrareṇu.
"Good Wealth (Sudhana) forgot his own body within the Dharma-realm; this is clearly stated in the scriptures and is not a mere speculative assertion.

May you have deep faith in the Buddha’s words and fortunately follow this clear guidance. The Chan Master is a dragon-elephant among the Buddhadharma; his pearl of precepts is perfectly pure, and the water of his concentration is profoundly serene.

Through stillness he gives rise to wisdom, and he possesses peaceful, unimpeded eloquence. He puts others first and himself last, having made humility and self-effacement his custom. His fame is heard afar, as is known by all."
I, [Your Disciple], have with devout sincerity directed my thoughts afar and extended an invitation from a distance. I have always feared that conditions might fail or various obstacles encountered;
yet now that you have arrived, the path of my mind has become clear and vast. As soon as the clouds and mist were dispelled, my afflictions were immediately extinguished.
On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month of the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era, I shall provide a meal for a thousand monks at the Jincheng Hall of the Governor-General’s residence.
I humbly request that you deign to bestow the Bodhisattva Precepts. These precepts are called filial piety, and they are also termed restraint. They are the skillful means of Prajñāpāramitā;

they take refuge in the ultimate source and honor the supreme. By means of this superior merit, I offer it to the Most Honorable Empress to serve as a great adornment, so that she may share the compassion of the Tathāgata and the universal love of all Buddhas, regarding the four modes of birth with equal vision as if they were her only child.

The *Bailu* (Record of a Hundred Items) contains the full commentary on the precepts, totaling over seven hundred characters; the current text abbreviates this to only three hundred and thirteen characters.
Regarding the "Instruction in the Courtyard": in the *Lunyu*, Chen Kang asked Bo Yu, saying, "Have you, sir, heard anything extraordinary?
He replied, "Not yet. Once, while [our father] was standing alone in the courtyard, I hurried past him. He said, 'Have you studied the Odes? I replied..."
"Not yet. Without studying the *Shi*, one has no means to speak. Li retired and studied the *Shi*. This continued until Li retired and studied the *Li*.
This is precisely the instruction given while approaching the courtyard. *Yí* (彝) is pronounced *yí*. Both the *Bǎilù* and the *Nánshān zhuàn* read it as such.
*Yí* is glossed as "to present" (*zèng*). Here, *yí* is glossed as "law" (*fǎ*). The meaning is thus correct. *Qíqū* (崎嶇) describes a winding or tortuous appearance; it serves as a metaphor.

The study of the Śrāvakas is like a small transformed city on a narrow path of three hundred *yojanas*; crossing to the other shore by boat is five hundred *yojanas*, whereby one ascends to the Precious Place (*ratnasthāna*).
The "ten receptions" refer to the ten precepts of the Brahma Net Sūtra. "Casting and forging" means melting gold with fire and using a mold to fashion an image;
through the teachings and regulations of the Three Vehicles, one studies and becomes a vessel. [He] bowed his head to bid farewell and invited him to come afar.
As for "The Great Master rested at Donglin Temple; the King was in Yangzhou and went to meet him by boat":

this refers to the metaphor of "dispelling clouds and mists so that afflictions are immediately extinguished. "Dispelling" (*pi*) means to open. It is like the opening of clouds and the rising of the sun. When the clouds part, the sun emerges.

The afflictions are like frost that withers [the flowers]. As for those who served and supported the Most Honorable Emperor and Empress—namely Emperor Wen and Lady Gudu—they were treated as if they were his only child.
Below this, there are ninety-five characters in the *Bai lu* (Records of a Hundred Matters) which have been omitted here.

The Master said, "Great King, you who follow the sacred prohibitions are called 'Total Retention' (Dhāraṇī). The King replied, 'Great Master, you who transmit the lamp of the Buddha-dharma are called 'The Wise One' (Jñānamitra).
The alms and offerings I have received, totaling sixty kinds, I now simultaneously bestow as gifts upon the two fields of compassion and reverence.'"
This caused his merit and virtue to increase, thereby benefiting his family and state.

Once the incense and lamp offerings were concluded, Prince Jin (Sui Yangdi) personally attended to him with great devotion, following the prohibitions of the Mahāyāna precepts: ceasing all evil and upholding all good;

thus it was called *dhāraṇī* (total retention). From the time he received the precepts, all his official records and writings referred to him by his Dharma name, while the Master himself was called Zhìzhě (the Wise One).
Therefore, the inscription on the stele of Guoqing Temple states: Later, King [Xuanzong] examined the *Dharmasaṃgraha-sūtra* and specifically established this title.

That sūtra’s tenth chapter, “The Chapter on Precepts,” says: “Whether a layperson or one who has left the home life, having made the vow for bodhi, one should reverently kneel and bow the body toward a wise person, saying these words:
‘I pray that the Virtuous One will accept my Bodhisattva Great Vinaya Precepts. As it continues...
Having formed this thought, he remained silent. At that time, the Wise One spoke these words: "O son of good family, you wish to receive from me all the great precepts of the bodhisattvas...
(and so forth). *Dāna* means giving (*śī*). *Dakṣiṇā* is translated here as "pure giving.
Although the characters differ, the meaning is one and the same. The text states there are sixty kinds for each; this should be changed to the word "shared" (*sādhāraṇa*).

Furthermore, as the fleet sailed across the Heng and Xia gorges, His Majesty the Great King provided a grand escort through Guizhou. He attended the departure by the river with such magnificent provisions that they were twice as lavish as before.
Encountering a favorable wind, the journey began in the morning and was completed by evening.
A large boat is called a *ge*. Regarding the two prefectures of Heng and Xia: they were originally south of Mount Nanyue in Hengzhou.
The mention of "Xia" refers to the location along the route. Heng is south of Lake Honghu (Jinghu) and Xia is north of Lake Honghu. As stated in the preceding biography:
when Master Si sought refuge from the troubles of the Zhou dynasty, he intended to reside at Mount Nanyue but temporarily stayed at Mount Sushan in Guangzhou, where Zhizhe received the Dharma.
Later, he went to Jiankang to practice the Way, but was unable to serve as an attendant. He longed to return to Mount Nanyue.
Since his [the Master's] passing into nirvana at Mount Nanyue, it was fitting that he should offer memorial sacrifices to repay the kindness of the Dharma-mother.

Thus, the Prince of Jin wrote in a letter: "I respectfully recall my temporary desire to travel west from Jiangling; I shall first proceed to Mount Heng to repay the Master’s grace. When the Prince’s carriage reached Yangzhou, he [received him].
As for those who saw him off, it is as recorded in the *Nanshan zhuan*: "After more than sixty matters had been settled, the King earnestly entreated him to stay.
Zhiyi said, 'There was a prior clear agreement; matters must not be double-crossed. He then shook his robe and rose. The King did not dare to invite him further.

As they walked together toward the city gate, he said, 'The state’s stability is no small matter, yet the affairs of the Way must be brought to completion. I hope you will observe the Buddha's transformation.'"
With the great protection [of the Dharma] held in his heart, King Li gazed at him until his vision failed; Heng returned with tears.
When Zhi returned, he left a letter in the *Bailu* (One Hundred Records) entrusting the King to compose the inscription for the Master of Mount Nanyue; the matter is very clear.
The officials and the laity of Zhugu looked up with necks outstretched, awaiting his arrival; old and young supported one another as they hurried toward the ordination platform.
Men with black hair and those already white, gathering like clouds, filled the lecture hall; the assembly numbered more than five thousand people.
Regarding the term *zhǔ* (渚): the *Erya* states, "That which can be inhabited within the water is called a *zhōu* (洲); the large ones are called *zhōu*, and the small ones are called *zhǔ*.

It is recorded that the region of Jingzhou was called Zhuguan; this designation already existed during the Spring and Autumn period. Du Yu did not understand it, and though he searched extensively through various books, he found no one who could explain it.
As for the current mention of an audience of over five thousand people, it is unknown in which monastery they were located.

It is likely that this passage concerning the construction of the Yuquan and Shizhu monasteries and the subsequent bestowal of the precepts refers to the period when the Great Master returned from Hengzhou;
at that time, officials and the laity along the river route all came out to welcome him, though Zhan’an has recorded it here only briefly.
The site of the Shixiang Monastery was unknown even in Jingzhou and Xiangyang. Now that the Sun of Wisdom has shone forth, a sanctuary of merit is about to be established.

A vihāra was built on Mount Yuquan in Dangyang County and, having received an imperial edict granting it a name, it was originally titled "Single Sound" (Yiyin), later changed again to "Jade Spring" (Yuquan).
This land was originally wild and perilous, where divine beasts and venomous snakes roamed; it was colloquially known as a thicket of the three poisons, chilling to those who stepped upon it.
As for the mind: during the interval of founding the temple, there was absolutely no cause for anxiety.
As for the location: it is like the Buddha’s preaching at the Deer Park and the Śāla Grove; all [these sites] are ways of repaying past kindnesses. Regarding Jingxiang:
Jingzhou was the ancient Nanyang Commandery, which was changed to Jiangling Prefecture and later to Xiangyang Prefecture; today it is Jingzhou.

The county of Dangyang belongs to Jiangling. When the Yuquan Temple was first established as Yinyin, it was granted the name "Yuquan" (Jade Spring) in the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era because the color of its water was like jade.
It is commonly heard that this temple was built through the supernatural power of Guan Yu, the former general of Shu; however, the *Record of Yuquan Temple* says nothing of this. Now, by chance...
He obtained the stele of the Jade Spring (Yùquán). It was said that Zhìzhě had reached Zhǔguān, ascended Nǎnjì, and gazed upon the mountain clouds. He specially established a *dōucháng* there;
observing that the colors of the Jǔzhàng mountains were piled like indigo and that purple clouds resembled a canopy, he wondered, "Is this a place where one may dwell?
Initially, he chose Qīngxī, but thinking it was too cramped and difficult to accommodate the multitude, he traveled more than one hundred [steps] north of Jīnlóngchí.
As he walked, there was a great tree with spreading branches and a canopy-like crown, its center hollow like a hut.
He then sat cross-legged beneath it in peaceful stillness and entered the Great Samādhi of Quiescence. One day, heaven and earth grew dark and gloomy, and wind and rain howled in fury.
Countless malevolent spirits appeared in various strange forms and wondrous shapes, crowding before the Master, intending to cause him harm. Furthermore, there was a giant...
A python over ten *zhang* long opened its mouth and bared its fangs, intending to devour him. Furthermore, demonic spirits of the dark realm drew up battle arrays, raining down firebombs and arrows.
For seven days, the Master showed no sign of fear. He took pity on them and said: "What you are doing is but a phantom dream of birth and death.
You are greedily attached to various karmic deeds and do not feel sorrow or repentance; why then do you come to harass me? Thus he spoke.
When it ended, they vanished without a trace. One night, the clouds and mist cleared away, and the moon shone as brightly as day.
Two holy beings appeared with a retinue whose dignified bearing was like that of kings: the elder had a fine beard and a robust appearance; the younger wore a cap and was strikingly handsome.
The Master then inquired of the holy ones, "From where have you come? They replied, "We are Guan [Yue], the former General of Shu."
My son, Nichihei, has long governed this region due to his meritorious service in battle. This mountain is known as Mount Sandoku;
from antiquity until the present, it is rarely visited by human footprints, serving only as a lair for dragons, snakes, tigers, leopards, and various spirits and demons.
Great Virtuous Master, why do you deign to trouble your divine feet? Since I passed through Tiantai, I have wished to [reside] here.
He established a site for a *bodhimaṇḍa* to offer a small measure of gratitude for the virtue of his parents’ procreation.
The deity said, “If this is truly so, disciple, you should establish a temple and solicit offerings to welcome the pure assembly from the ten directions.
One *shè* (li) from here, there is a mountain shaped like an overturned boat; its soil is deep and thick, and its geomantic potential is flourishing. Disciple, build the temple here.”
"I pray that you, Master, enter meditative concentration for seven days. Having spoken, he withdrew. Once the Master emerged from concentration, the great hall was completed.
*Pián* and *nán* timber were interlaced; the roof structure was towering and majestic; the vermilion and blue glazes were brilliant and vivid, with gold and turquoise reflecting one another.

He invited the Master to reside there and gathered a multitude to expound the Dharma. One day, the spirit said: "In the past, when I was a disciple, I used military force to wage war, carving up livers and [butchering] horns..."
Formerly indulging in flesh and unrestrained by greed and anger, what good fortune has he found today!

Having heard the unsurpassed, world-transcending Dharma of Bodhi, he now purifies his heart and cleanses his thoughts to seek the categories of precepts, forever sheltering himself under the Buddha-vehicle to ride upon its teachings to transform all living beings.

The Master acceded to his request and, holding the incense burner for him, transmitted the rites. From this time forth, his purity became even more refined and brilliant. (The above is from the front inscription.)
[This is the end of the] text). Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume 27, states: "As for Shi Faxing, his speech was often extraordinary.

He sometimes dwelt in mountain valleys, yet occasionally entered the marketplace. Whenever he went to Qingxi, his route passed over the summit of Fuhuan Mountain; there he beheld flowing springs and luxuriant trees."
He then looked back and said, "Ten years hence, there shall be a person of great merit and wisdom who will establish a monastery;
this is the coming of Zhizhe. Indeed, he has fulfilled what was previously foretold. Now it is known that Master Xingxian anticipated this intention beforehand;
he is truly a sage. "Decided" means determined. Since the three poisons have already been subdued, what cause for anxiety or concern could there be?

During a drought in the spring and summer, the common people all believed it was the wrath of the gods. Therefore, the Wise One went in person to the source of the spring to extinguish this false view;

he personally chanted prayers with his mouth, while his hand gestured and directed the way. Following the direction of his pointing, heavy clouds gathered like billowing curtains to envelop the mountains, and a long, brilliant rainbow rose from the spring.
Wind and rain surged forth in abundance, and songs of praise filled the roads.
At that time, a dragon occupied the territory. The Wise One (Zhìzhě) established Yùquán (Jade Spring) beside the Golden Dragon Pond;
however, the dragon became enraged and withheld rain. Regarding the term "huīlüè" (撝略): "huī" means to point toward or grasp, and "lüè" means method; this refers to the practice of reciting dhāraṇīs.
Wang Ji, the Generalissimo of Jingzhou, Grand Marshal of State, and Duke of Yiyang, arrived at the mountain to pay his respects. He was trembling with fear and felt deeply unsettled.
Stepping outside, he said: "I have experienced many military campaigns and have been even more courageous when facing danger; never before have I been as terrified as I am this day."
The *Suí Shū*, Biographies Volume V, states: Wang Shijī was a native of Chǎnxī Xīnqùn [Zhōngwén].

His father, Yǎ, served as a Grand Master of the Household with the title of "Knight of the State" (Kāiguó Yítóng Sānsī) under the Northern Zhōu dynasty. Shijī was of imposing stature, his waist measuring ten spans in circumference.
Feng Shen was distinguished and eminent, possessing the bearing of a superior man. When the High Ancestor received the abdication of the throne, he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Yiyang.

After the subjugation of Chen, he was promoted to the rank of Pillar of State (Zhuguo) and appointed as the Regional Inspector (Zongduan) of Jingzhou. When the expedition to Liaodong was launched, he served as the Commander-in-Chief (Xingjun Yuanshuai).
Upon reaching Liucheng, he fell ill and returned; he was subsequently appointed as the Regional Inspector of Liangzhou. His plot to rebel was exposed, and he was executed for his crimes.
In that year, the King sent an envoy to welcome him.
On the twenty-second day of the second month of the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era, Emperor Wen summoned the Master to court.
Therefore, the record states: "This disciple is now entering the capital for an audience; while traveling through Xiazhou, my sincere longing increases with the passing time."

Because [the King] had accumulated [merit], he dispatched an envoy to welcome him, hoping that [the Master] would immediately proceed on his journey. Toward the end of the month, he was merely awaiting the formal reception;

the details of the correspondence are recorded in the *Bai lu* (Records of the Hundred) and need not be written here in full. Although King [Xiao Ziliang] had received the precepts in the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era, his underlying purpose remained unfulfilled.
At that time, Zhizhe was urgently preparing for his travels to Mount Heng and Jingzhou, and thus departed in haste. King...
Since I have already gazed upon you, I have come once more to welcome you.
The people of Jing have failed to attend your audience; they offer their distant salutations toward the direction from which you come.

In the past, when the Dharma King appeared in the world, he relied upon the purity of a single path and expounded with a single voice;

yet, as the capacities and responses of sentient beings differed, what they heard was likewise diverse. Thus arose the meanings of the five periods, the five flavors, the provisional and the complete, the expedient and the real, the partial and the perfect, and the small and the great.
Disseminated across various schools, these diverse streams flow in different directions; yet, as for their ultimate destination, none transcend the single reality (*eka-tattva*).
Thus, the Sūtra says: "Though various paths are taught, in truth they constitute the Buddha-vehicle. It further states: "Opening the gate of skillful means, it reveals the mark of reality.

This is illustrated by the metaphor of many rivers flowing into the sea and signaled by the Gate of Non-duality (*advaya-dvāra*). Both self and others attain [enlightenment], together arriving at the secret treasury.

This is the origin of the Esoteric (Mystic) teachings. When the Nirvana at the Crane Forest (Hailing) was manifested, the framework of the Dharma fell into disarray; as the divine powers vanished, the paths of the schools diverged.

Each party relied upon its own provisional authority, and their disputes became as sharp as clashing spears. Among them, there were those who attained birth through samādhi and those who appeared as the four reliances (catur-apāśraya);

These various schools branched out along separate paths, and their discourses on that which is neither existence nor emptiness could not be unified.

Subsequently, as the distance from the Sage grew ever greater, this trend spread eastward. Those who expounded the Dharma were shackled by words and characters, unable to find liberation for themselves;

those who practiced meditation became lost in the void regarding the nature and characteristics of phenomena, incapable of being drawn back to the truth. Thus, they disparaged one side while praising the other, and those who had abandoned realization claimed to have attained it.
The Way of wisdom and liberation flowed forth until people forgot its source; the conduct of body and speech became dissolute and lacked discipline.
